name: Freya Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day looks like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I build mobile apps at Clubhaus, a startup of about forty people that makes booking and membership apps for gyms, swimming pools and sports clubs. I start around eight with a coffee and set two or three AI agents going on tasks, like fixing a bug in the class-booking screen or writing tests, and then I review what they've done. The afternoon is calls with club managers, who always want one more button. I probably write a third of the code by hand that I did two years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love shipping things fast and seeing a club manager's face when the feature they asked for on Monday is live by Thursday. What wears me out is the startup money worry, because we live from one funding round to the next. Weekends I'm usually on my boyfriend Tobias's family dairy farm, an hour out of town, and that's my reset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be surprised. I'm already seeing much more than that in my own work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are good, but businesses still win on knowing their customers and working hard. I'd post a bit about the gap between hype and what the tools really do. At the farm I'd joke that Tobias's cows were never in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. I'm faster than most of my colleagues because I use the tools well, and that edge doesn't disappear in a slow world. Clubhaus might struggle to raise money, but good mobile developers can find work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and ask for a raise at review time in January, using my shipped features as proof. I'd keep about five months of costs in savings and put another three hundred a month into a share fund. Tobias and I would get engaged next year as we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by how ordinary it would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the startup money worry. Does that change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that stays. Clubhaus has about fourteen months of money left, and if the next round fails, we all look for work. I'm not scared of that, because I've got savings and other startups in town would hire me. But it's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tasks AI takes over affect anyone on your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our support person, Jonas, answers club managers' emails all day. Some of that would go to a chatbot even in a slow world. I'd help him move into setting up new clubs, which needs a person on the phone.

I'd post about the **gap between hype** and what the tools really do.
think: My **speed with the tools** keeps me ahead of most colleagues even in a slow world.
Clubhaus might **struggle to raise money**, but good mobile developers find work.
do: Ask for a **raise in January**, using shipped features as proof.
Keep **five months** of savings and add 300 monthly to a share fund.
Get **engaged** to Tobias next year, as planned.
feel: **Calm**, a bit **bored** by how ordinary it would be.

fieldNote: She is already **ahead of this picture** in her own daily work with agents.
Her standing pressure is the startup's **funding runway**, which she treats calmly.
She looks out for **Jonas**, the support colleague whose emails could go to a chatbot.

steps.text: Ask for a raise at the January review using shipped features
Put 300 a month into a share fund
Get engaged to Tobias next year as planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. That's the one I think we're actually living in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who learn the tools will be fine and the people who refuse will struggle, and that's how it's always been with new tools. At work I'd run lunchtime sessions showing my set-up. Online I'd say competition makes everyone better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm on the safe side of it, but some colleagues aren't. Clubhaus would probably go from twelve developers to eight, and the cuts would fall on the people who still type everything by hand. That's hard, because a couple of them are friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to lead the AI tooling for the whole team, because that's the role they'd keep. I'd keep saving, five hundred a month, and put a bit more into shares, maybe in the companies making these tools. I'd also start a small side project, a booking app for farm shops, with Tobias's mum as my first customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for my friends, energised for myself. It's an odd mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Nadia, mainly. She's a careful developer, better at architecture than me, but she won't touch the agents. I've tried to show her twice. I'd try a third time, but I can't make her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said competition makes everyone better. Would you say that to Nadia's face?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gently, yes. I believe in competition, but I don't think people should be left with nothing. Nadia has a degree, savings and a good brain. I'd tell my colleague Nadia she has six months to learn the tools before someone else decides for her.

say: I'd say people who **learn the tools** do fine, as with every new tool.
I'd run **lunchtime sessions** at work and say **competition** improves everyone.
think: I'm on the **safe side**, but Clubhaus could drop from twelve developers to eight.
The cuts would hit colleagues who **type everything by hand**, including friends.
do: Ask to **lead AI tooling** for the whole development team.
Save **500 a month** and put more into shares in AI tool makers.
Start a **farm-shop booking app** with Tobias's mum as first customer.
feel: **Uneasy** for my friends and **energised** for myself, an odd mix.
S1.quote: I'd tell my colleague Nadia she has six months to learn the tools before someone else decides for her.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **safe**, so her unease is about **colleagues** like Nadia.
She holds **free-market views** but stops short of leaving people with nothing.
She spots a **side business** in farm-shop bookings through Tobias's family.

steps.text: Ask to lead AI tooling for Clubhaus's developers
Buy shares in companies that make AI coding tools
Build a farm-shop booking app with Tobias's mum as first customer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That changes things even for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a huge chance for anyone who owns something, a business, land, machines. I'd tell people to stop waiting for the government to fix it. At work I'd be honest that our jobs are on a short clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my developer job is gone by 2029. Being good with the tools only buys me a year, because AGI doesn't need someone like me to steer it. The farm is hands-on, so it gets until about 2031, and it's land, which is something you own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Tobias and his parents about putting my savings, around twelve thousand, into the farm, maybe towards a milking robot or an automated feeding system. I'd keep working at Clubhaus as long as they'd pay me and save nearly all of it. We'd bring the wedding forward and I'd move out to the farm to stop paying city rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I'd feel the ground moving, and I'd want to be standing on something solid when it stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Investing in robots for the farm, when robots are what's coming. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd rather own the robot than compete with it. A milking robot on a dairy farm frees the farmer to run a bigger herd. If the robots are coming anyway, the farmers who bought early and know how to run them will be the last ones standing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The city flat, the gym membership, eating out on Fridays. And probably my idea of being a developer until I'm fifty. That one stings more than the flat.

say: I'd say it's a huge chance for anyone who **owns something**: a business, land or machines.
I'd tell people to **stop waiting** for government and be honest our jobs are on a short clock.
think: I expect my developer job **gone by 2029**; tool skills only buy one year.
The **farm** is hands-on land we own, safe until about 2031.
do: Invest about **12,000 of savings** in a milking robot or feeding system on the farm.
Keep working at Clubhaus and **save nearly everything** while it lasts.
Bring the **wedding forward** and move to the farm to stop paying rent.
feel: **Anxious** but awake, wanting **solid ground** when things stop moving.
S2.quote: I'd rather own the robot than compete with it. A milking robot on a dairy farm frees the farmer to run a bigger herd.
fieldNote: She admits her **tool edge** won't save her and expects to lose the job by 2029.
Her answer is **ownership**: invest savings in robots on her boyfriend's family farm.
Giving up her picture of a **long developer career** hurts more than losing the flat.

steps.text: Put about 12,000 into a milking robot on Tobias's family farm
Save nearly all of her Clubhaus pay while the job lasts
Give up the city flat and move to the farm
Bring the wedding with Tobias forward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to do this properly instead of in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift, so use it. I'd encourage people to buy into something real, like a business or land, instead of just saving cash. Online I'd write about my own plan, because people learn from examples.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job goes around 2030 or 2031, but by then I'd want to be somewhere else. I'd have three years of dev pay saved and invested, a farm with the right machines, and skills in running them. It's not a disaster for me, it's a career change I'd have chosen anyway in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep developing at Clubhaus for three more years and save hard, about eight hundred a month. I'd take an agricultural technology course on weekends so I understand milking robots and herd software, not just apps. We'd marry in 2027 and I'd move to the farm in 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. I'd be nervous about telling my parents I'm leaving tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why nervous about your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drove a tram for thirty years so I could go to university. Telling my dad I'm going to a farm feels like throwing that away. I'd explain the degree is why I can run the robots, and I think he'd get it eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your side project in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the farm-shop app small and use it to learn what farms actually need. By 2029 it might have twenty farm shops on it. It won't survive AGI, but it'd pay for a lot of fence repairs before then.

say: I'd say five years is a **gift**, so people should use it.
I'd urge people to **buy into something real**, and share my own plan online.
think: My job likely **ends around 2031**, but I'd plan to have moved on by then.
It's a **career change** I'd have chosen in ten years anyway, not a disaster.
do: Stay at Clubhaus **three more years**, saving about 800 a month.
Take a weekend **agricultural technology course** on milking robots and herd software.
Marry Tobias in **2027** and move to the farm in 2029.
feel: **Uneasy** but mostly **hopeful**, nervous about telling my parents I'm leaving tech.
S3.quote: My dad drove a tram for thirty years so I could go to university. Telling my dad I'm going to a farm feels like throwing that away.
fieldNote: With five years, she sees her own future as a **chosen move**, not a loss.
Her worry shifts to **family pride**: her tram-driver father paid for her degree.
She'd use the **farm-shop app** to learn farming needs and fund repairs.

steps.text: Save about 800 a month during three more years at Clubhaus
Take a weekend course on milking robots and herd software
Marry Tobias in 2027 and move to the farm in 2029
Grow the farm-shop booking app to about twenty shops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's easy to plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career for some people, so there's no excuse not to prepare. I'd still say competition and hard work are what get you through. I'd tell younger developers to own something by the time they're forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one looks good for me. I'd have years of good pay, the tools make me faster, and Tobias's family farm would be ours to run by then. Robots on the farm arrive in 2039, and we'd own them rather than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Clubhaus or a similar company for five or six years and push for a lead developer role. I'd keep investing three to five hundred a month in shares. Tobias and I would marry and try for children around thirty-one, and I'd move to the farm part-time from about 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in that picture that does worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices, maybe. If everyone's buying land and machines to get ready, milk prices and land prices could do strange things. And I can't control what the government does with taxes on robots. But that's a business worry, not a fear for my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a colleague who isn't preparing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade sounds long until it isn't. Most people I know will wait until year eight. I'd tell them to sign up for one course this year, any course, just to start.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** not to prepare.
I'd tell younger developers to **own something** by forty.
think: This picture looks **good for me**: years of pay, then a farm we own.
We'd **own the farm robots** in 2039 rather than be replaced by them.
do: Push for a **lead developer** role over five or six years.
Keep investing **300 to 500** a month in shares.
Marry, try for **children** around 31, and move to the farm part-time from 2032.
S4.quote: A decade sounds long until it isn't. Most people I know will wait until year eight.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees **opportunity**, not threat, and plans to own farm machines.
Her remaining concerns are **business risks**: land prices, milk prices and robot taxes.
Her advice is blunt: **start one course** now rather than wait until year eight.

steps.text: Push for a lead developer role at Clubhaus
Invest 300 to 500 a month in shares
Marry Tobias and try for children around 31
Move to the farm part-time from about 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to set things up properly. I'd be putting my savings into a farm in a hurry, and hurry is how people lose money. What would help is clear rules early, especially on taxes for robots and land, so people like us can plan. I don't want a handout, I want to know the rules of the game.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd look after the people who can't adapt. I believe in standing on your own feet, but I've watched my colleague Nadia, and some people need more time than the market gives them. Families and towns will have to carry them.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want to know the rules of the game.

She stays **calm or uneasy** in slow pictures and anxious only when AGI arrives by 2028.
Her plan is **ownership**: invest in robots on her boyfriend Tobias's family dairy farm.
She believes in **competition** but worries about colleagues like Nadia who won't adapt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which would force her to invest savings in the farm in a hurry.
